analysis.one_liner: Bans medical debt on credit reports and shortens how long most negative information stays.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House and referred to the Financial Services Committee, where it received no hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules of consumer credit reporting. It would ban medical debt from credit reports entirely, cut the time most negative information stays on a report (for example, bankruptcies from 10 years to 7 and collections from 7 to 4), require paid or settled debts to come off within 45 days, and erase the credit damage done to people who were cheated by predatory mortgage lenders, for-profit schools, or financial abusers. It would also give free credit monitoring to seniors, unemployed people, servicemembers, and fraud victims, and require credit bureaus to set a fair fee for everyone else.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially the roughly one in five whose reports carry medical collections, people who paid off old debts, borrowers cheated by predatory mortgage lenders or for-profit schools, domestic abuse survivors whose credit was wrecked by an abuser, seniors, unemployed people, and victims of identity theft.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with damaged or medical-debt-laden credit

how_it_helps.text: Bans medical debt from consumer credit reports, ending a practice that can unfairly lower a score by up to 22 points even after the bill is paid, according to Consumer Bureau research cited in the bill's findings.

Cuts how long negative information stays on a report: bankruptcies from 10 years to 7, collections and tax liens from 7 years to 4, and requires fully paid or settled debts to be removed within 45 days.

Removes adverse information from the reports of people who were victimized by predatory mortgage lending or servicing, by fraud at for-profit schools, or by financial abuse from a partner or family member, once a court or agency has found wrongdoing or the consumer submits documentation.

Gives free credit monitoring and identity theft protection to fraud victims, unemployed people, public assistance recipients, active-duty military, and people 65 or older, and requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to set a fair and reasonable fee for everyone else.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion), debt collectors and debt buyers, credit monitoring sellers, and lenders, who would lose information they currently use to price credit and lose revenue from paid-for monitoring and longer-lived collections entries.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, monitoring sellers

drawbacks.text: With less delinquency history on reports, lenders would have less information to judge risk, which could mean higher rates or tighter credit standards for some borrowers overall, the trade-off any reporting restriction creates.

Paid or settled debts vanishing from reports within 45 days removes information that helps other lenders price credit, a change an honest supporter would acknowledge shifts risk assessment and could blunt the accountability value of credit reporting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is large and concrete: medical debt is the single biggest category of collections on credit reports, it has little value in predicting repayment, and people who pay a bill in full can still see their score punished for it. Cutting the reporting clock for old debts and helping defrauded and abused consumers rebuild credit are real but narrower gains. The cost is that lenders see a thinner credit history, which may raise pricing slightly for some borrowers; on balance the benefits outweigh that cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill in the House on August 8, 2023.
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The bill received no further action: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and it expired at the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, and companies selling credit monitoring are better off, since the rules that let medical bills and paid debts linger on reports, and let them charge for monitoring, stayed in place. Consumers with medical debt or blemished credit gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban medical debt from credit reports and shorten reporting periods.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic (Tlaib plus 4 Democratic cosponsors), and the Republican-controlled House never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill would cut data they sell to lenders (shorter reporting periods, no medical debt, 45-day removal of paid debts) and force them to give free monitoring to large classes of consumers and charge others only a CFPB-set fee. Their interest in keeping reports full and their paid products alive runs against consumers' interest in clean, accurate reports.

They decide when and how long a collection appears on a report; the bill would shorten that window to 4 years and require removal within 45 days of payment, shrinking their leverage over consumers who dispute or pay.

industries.industry: Credit monitoring and identity protection sellers
industries.note: The bill would give free monitoring to seniors, the unemployed, servicemembers, and fraud victims and cap what bureaus can charge others, undercutting a market the bill's findings say companies grew with 'free' offers that auto-converted into subscriptions.

industries.industry: For-profit colleges and private student lenders
industries.note: Borrowers defrauded by proprietary schools would get the related loan's adverse information wiped from their reports, erasing the default trail that currently follows those students.
Consumers harmed by unfair, deceptive, or fraudulent mortgage servicing would get the related foreclosures and delinquencies removed from their reports.
